screens.title: Private Data Collections (PDC)
screens.narratorSegment: In permissioned blockchains, knowing the participants doesn't automatically solve confidentiality. Private Data Collections let a subset of channel members exchange sensitive information peer-to-peer while the channel ledger remains auditable. In this lesson you will learn why PDCs exist, how Fabric keeps private data off the public world state, and how a hash on the public ledger preserves integrity without revealing secrets. We will also walk through how to configure collections, how chaincode stores and retrieves private records, and common operational pitfalls to avoid. Picture a supply chain where price or reserve offers must remain visible only to trading partners: PDCs make that selective sharing practical. By the end you will be able to define a collection in a collections. json file, call PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData from chaincode, and reason about the trade-offs between privacy, auditability and data lifecycle. As you progress, think about which parts of an application truly need persistent privacy and which can remain public. That decision guides your collection design and operational choices.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Private Data Collections
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Private Data Collections

Selective private storage for a subset of channel members, with a public hash for verification.

Why it matters

Keep commercially sensitive fields private while preserving an auditable public record. This enables compliance, selective sharing, and reduced trust surface.

When to use

Use PDCs when only some organizations should store or query a secret, for example prices, bids, or personally identifiable fields in a consortium network.

Explore Key Topics
Collections Config
Define members, counts, and blockToLive in a JSON file.
Private State DB
Private data lives on authorized peers, separate from the public world state.
Public Hash
Fabric commits a hash of private data to the ledger to ensure integrity without revealing secrets.
Concept map
private ↔ public
Authorized Peers

Store confidential records in the private state database for the collection.

Public Ledger

Receives only a hash of private data for audit and integrity checks.

Chaincode API

Use PutPrivateData, GetPrivateData and DelPrivateData to interact with collections.

Collections Config

collection_config.json defines membership, counts and lifetimes.

This map highlights the separation between private storage and public proof. Think of the hash as a receipt you can show everyone while keeping the content private.

First, you will explain when PDCs are necessary and list common use cases, including selective sharing in supply chains and financial consortia. Knowing the why helps you avoid overuse. Second, you will define collections in a collection_config. json file: you will identify the name, membership policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, and blockToLive, and understand how these settings affect distribution and retention. Third, you will implement chaincode to interact with private collections using PutPrivateData, GetPrivateData and DelPrivateData, and you will learn to use the transient field to keep inputs out of the public ledger. Fourth, you will analyze how private data affects the ledger: where private state lives, what the public hash guarantees, and how mismatched state or misconfigured policies can invalidate transactions. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can check competency with a concrete task, such as writing a collections. json and demonstrating GetPrivateData from an authorized peer.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical checks
screens.narratorSegment: These practical checks turn knowledge into demonstrable skills. For configuration, create a collections. json that names a collection, sets an OR-style policy for member MSPs, and chooses required and maximum peer counts; deploy a chaincode commit that uses the file and confirm no errors appear. For code, add functions that marshal a private struct and call PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData; then run a test where an authorized peer reads the private record and an unauthorized peer cannot. For transient usage, send input in a transient map and confirm that the private content never appears in the transaction payload recorded in the public ledger; only a hash is present. For lifecycle, set blockToLive in one collection and observe that peers purge the private entry after the specified number of blocks in a controlled test network. Each check focuses on a single failure mode so you can isolate issues: wrong MSP IDs, incorrect commit flags, or passing confidential data in the public payload. These checks are short, repeatable, and directly validate the learning objectives.

screens.title: Why PDCs exist
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Fabric channels provide a shared ledger where every organization's peers see the world state. That model is simple and powerful, but it isn't sufficient when business rules require selective confidentiality. Private Data Collections exist to fill that gap. A PDC is a logical collection defined on a channel that limits which peers receive and store certain data. The private data itself lives in a private state database on authorized peers, while Fabric stores a hash of that private data on the public ledger. That hash provides immutable evidence that a transaction involving private data occurred, so the network retains verifiability without exposing secrets. Consider a manufacturer and a supplier negotiating raw material costs: price should be private to the negotiating parties while shipment IDs remain public for tracking. PDCs enable exactly that. A common misconception is to treat PDCs as encryption; they are not encryption services. PDC access is governed by membership and endorsement rules. If you need stronger protection in transit or at rest, combine PDCs with TLS and storage encryption, but rely on the PDC model for selective distribution and auditability. When designing a network, decide which attributes must be private and which can be public; that decision drives collection membership and policy design.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: PDCs let a subset of channel organizations store confidential data privately while a hash is recorded publicly for integrity.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Why PDCs exist
Definition

A Private Data Collection restricts which peers receive and store specific data while the channel ledger keeps a hash for verification.

Key bullets
  • Private data stored only on authorized peers' private state DB.
  • A hash of the private data is committed to the public ledger for auditability.
  • PDCs are about selective distribution, not encryption services.
Key Takeaway

Use PDCs to limit which organizations store and read sensitive fields while preserving verifiability for all channel members.

Concrete scenario

Manufacturer A sells to Distributor B. The price is private between A and B but the asset ID and shipment details remain public. PDCs allow storing the price only on A and B peers while the ledger holds a hash of that private price to prove the transaction occurred.

Common misconception

PDCs do not automatically encrypt private data for everyone; they control who stores it. Encryption and other protections may still be applied as needed.

Why it matters

Enables business privacy while keeping auditability and consistency guarantees.

Question

Which asset attributes in your application must be private versus public?

screens.title: How private data is stored and proven
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric separates the storage of private content from the public world state. Authorized peers keep private entries in a private state database, such as CouchDB or LevelDB. When a transaction includes private data, Fabric writes the private content to those peers' private state DB and computes a hash of that content to be written into the public ledger. That hash acts as an immutable proof linking the public transaction to private content without exposing it. If a peer later tries to commit a transaction whose private data hash does not match the hash on the ledger, the transaction will be marked invalid. This automatic consistency check prevents tampering or mismatched state between peers. Another important architectural point is that the collection's policy controls who receives the private payload during endorsement and commit. Endorsement policies for the chaincode still apply to the transaction; the PDC policy controls distribution of the private data, not endorsement. A misconception is to assume the PDC policy replaces endorsement rules. They operate independently: endorsements decide whether a transaction is valid; collection policies decide which peers store and can query the private data. Think of the public hash as a commitment and the private state DB as the secure vault.

keyIdea.title: Architecture insight
keyIdea.text: Private content resides on authorized peers; a public hash preserves integrity and detects mismatches without exposing the data.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Private storage & proof
Private State Database

Authorized peers store private records locally in a private state DB. This keeps confidential fields off the public world state.

  • Private content written to private DB on authorized peers.
  • Fabric computes and commits a hash of the private content to the public ledger.
  • Ledger hash enables verification without revealing private fields.
Watch out

A mismatch between private data and the public hash invalidates the transaction; Fabric enforces consistency automatically.

Distribution vs Endorsement

Collection policies control who receives private payloads. Chaincode endorsement policies still govern transaction endorsement and must be satisfied regardless of PDC membership.

Example

A transaction with private price data will be endorsed and sent to peers defined by the collection policy; the public ledger stores a hash. Later, any peer can verify the ledger hash against private data if they hold it.

Misconception

PDC policies do not replace chaincode endorsement policies; they are complementary controls used for distribution and endorsement respectively.

screens.title: collection_config.json fields
screens.narratorSegment: The collection configuration file is the authoritative definition of a Private Data Collection. Each field has operational consequences you must consider. The name is a unique identifier used by chaincode when calling PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData. The policy is an endorsement-style expression that lists member MSP IDs; it determines which organizations are authorized to receive and store private data. requiredPeerCount is the minimum number of peers that must successfully commit private data for the write to be considered validated; set it to a value that reflects your durability needs. maxPeerCount limits how many peers will receive the private payload—useful to reduce exposure. blockToLive sets the lifespan of private entries in the private DB in blocks; zero means retain forever, while a non-zero value will cause automatic purging after the specified number of blocks. Picking blockToLive helps meet privacy or retention requirements but remember that the public hash remains on the ledger even after private data is purged. Common mistakes include incorrect MSP IDs in the policy that prevent rightful members from accessing data and inconsistent counts that cause unexpected commit failures. Always validate your policy strings and test access from each intended member before deploying to production.

keyIdea.title: Config fields
keyIdea.text: Name, policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount and blockToLive determine membership, distribution, durability, and retention for a collection.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › collection_config.json fields
Field reference
name
Unique collection identifier used by chaincode calls.
policy
Membership policy listing MSP IDs that are authorized to receive private data.
requiredPeerCount
Minimum number of peers that must commit private data for the write to be valid.
maxPeerCount
Maximum peers to which the private payload will be sent.
blockToLive
Number of blocks to retain the private data on private DB; 0 means keep forever. The public hash remains regardless.
Practical notes
  • Verify MSP IDs in policy match organization MSPs exactly to avoid access errors.
  • Set requiredPeerCount to reflect how many peers must have the private entry for durability guarantees.
  • Use blockToLive for temporary secrets; remember the public hash will persist.
Common mistake

Mis-typed MSP IDs in the policy prevent authorized peers from receiving private data. Double-check exact MSP strings.

screens.title: Example collections.json
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at a concrete collections. json example and interpret it. The file can define multiple collection objects. The first collection, named assetPrivateDetailsCollection, uses a policy allowing Org1 and Org2 members, sets requiredPeerCount to one and maxPeerCount to two, and keeps private data indefinitely with blockToLive set to zero. This setup suits a durable private record shared by two organizations. The second collection, assetBidCollection, allows Org2 and Org3 and sets blockToLive to one hundred blocks, which is useful for temporary bidding information that should expire. When you commit chaincode that uses these collections, include the file via the --collections-config flag. A common error is forgetting to include the file during chaincode commit, which means peers will not have the collection metadata and private data distribution will fail. Also, collection names must match what chaincode uses when calling PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData; otherwise the chaincode will fail to find the collection. Use this example as a template and adjust policies and retention to your business rules. Example collections.json means example shows one persistent collection for private details and one temporary collection for bids with a limited blocktolive.. In practical terms, two collections with different lifetimes and membership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Example collections.json
collections.json (excerpt)
[
  {
    "name": "assetPrivateDetailsCollection",
    "policy": "OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member')",
    "requiredPeerCount": 1,
    "maxPeerCount": 2,
    "blockToLive": 0
  },
  {
    "name": "assetBidCollection",
    "policy": "OR('Org2MSP.member', 'Org3MSP.member')",
    "requiredPeerCount": 1,
    "maxPeerCount": 3,
    "blockToLive": 100
  }
]
Interpretation
  • First collection: persistent private details shared by Org1 and Org2.
  • Second collection: bids shared by Org2 and Org3 with a finite lifespan of 100 blocks.
  • Remember to supply this file during chaincode commit with --collections-config.
Key Takeaway

Collections define who stores private data and how long it lives; align them to your privacy and retention requirements.

screens.title: Chaincode APIs for PDC
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode interacts with Private Data Collections through a small set of specialized APIs provided by the stub. PutPrivateData stores a value under a key in a named collection, GetPrivateData retrieves that private value for authorized peers, and DelPrivateData removes it from the private state database. These calls behave like PutState/GetState/DelState but are scoped to a collection. It is important to pass private inputs via the client transient map for confidentiality; the chaincode should read sensitive fields from the transient map and then call PutPrivateData. If you pass sensitive data directly as transaction arguments, those arguments may be visible in transaction proposals and could be recorded or exposed. Another critical point is error handling: GetPrivateData can return nil when the private value is not found or the peer is not authorized; chaincode should return clear errors in that case. Finally, remember that DelPrivateData only deletes the private entry from private DB—the hash remains on the ledger. Use these APIs consistently and combine them with proper authorization checks, such as verifying the client's MSP ID before writing private details. Chaincode APIs for PDC means use putprivatedata/getprivatedata/delprivatedata to manage private entries; always prefer transient inputs for confidentiality.. In practical terms, putprivatedata, getprivatedata and delprivatedata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Chaincode APIs for PDC
API summary
// Store private data
stub.PutPrivateData(collectionName, key, value)

// Retrieve private data
stub.GetPrivateData(collectionName, key)

// Delete private data
stub.DelPrivateData(collectionName, key)
  • These calls are scoped to the named collection.
  • Use transient map for confidential inputs and then PutPrivateData.
  • DelPrivateData removes private data but the public hash remains.
Practical pattern

Read confidential inputs from the transient map, do authorization checks, marshal the private struct, then call PutPrivateData. For retrieval, handle nil results gracefully and provide descriptive errors when data is absent or unauthorized.

Pitfall

Putting private content in transaction arguments risks exposing it in proposal responses. Use transient for secrecy.

screens.title: SetAssetPrivateDetails — chaincode example
screens.narratorSegment: This code pattern shows the core steps for storing private details for an asset. First, the chaincode obtains the submitting client's MSP ID to verify they are authorized to make the change. This is a simple authorization check; collection policies provide stronger governance but application checks are a useful additional layer. Next, the private struct is marshaled to JSON bytes. Then the stub's PutPrivateData is called with the collection name and asset key. In production you should retrieve sensitive fields from the transient map instead of passing them directly; that prevents them appearing in proposal payloads. Also handle marshal and Put errors explicitly to surface failures. Finally, you may want to write a public marker or metadata to the world state indicating a private payload exists without revealing content—the hash is automatically committed by Fabric, so you do not need to explicitly compute or store it. This example captures the pattern of authenticate, marshal, and persist to a named collection, and it provides a clear point of failure to instrument in tests when access is misconfigured. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › SetAssetPrivateDetails
Go example (excerpt)
type AssetPrivateDetails struct {
  Price     float64 `json:"price"`
  BuyerMSP  string  `json:"buyerMSP"`
  SellerMSP string  `json:"sellerMSP"`
}

// Verify client MSP, marshal and store private data
err = ctx.GetStub().PutPrivateData("assetPrivateDetailsCollection", assetID, privateDetailsBytes)
Explanation
  • Check client MSP to ensure only authorized submitters set private details.
  • Marshal the struct to bytes and call PutPrivateData with the correct collection name.
  • Prefer transient map inputs for true confidentiality from client applications.
Example takeaway

This pattern enforces simple authorization and keeps private data off the public world state while still allowing ledger-level verification via the public hash.

screens.title: GetAssetPrivateDetails — retrieval and errors
screens.narratorSegment: Retrieving private data requires similar care. When a peer calls GetPrivateData for a collection and key, the stub returns the private bytes if the peer is authorized and the data exists. If the result is nil, it may indicate either the data was never stored, was purged due to blockToLive, or the calling peer is not authorized to access it. Your chaincode should distinguish these cases where possible and return helpful error messages. After obtaining the bytes, unmarshal into the struct and validate fields. Also handle JSON unmarshal errors in case of schema drift. A common mistake is assuming nil always means the asset doesn't exist; in a PDC scenario nil can mean access is unauthorized. screens.title: Deploying chaincode with collections
screens.narratorSegment: When you deploy or upgrade chaincode that uses Private Data Collections, the lifecycle commit step must be supplied with the collections configuration file. The peer lifecycle chaincode commit command accepts a --collections-config flag pointing to your collections. json. This ensures that peers in the channel record the collection metadata as part of the chaincode definition and know which peers should receive private payloads. If you omit the collections file at commit time, peers will not have the collection definition and private data operations will fail at runtime. The deployment process typically looks like packaging the chaincode, approving definitions from organizations, and when the definition is committed, supply --collections-config./collections. json. After commit, confirm that each intended peer has the collection metadata and test PutPrivateData to validate distribution. A common deployment mistake is modifying the collections file and not performing a chaincode upgrade with the updated collections metadata; collection changes require lifecycle updates so update procedures should be planned and coordinated among consortium members. Deploying chaincode with collections means always include --collections-config during chaincode commit so peers learn the collection metadata and private data distribution works correctly.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Retention and deletion
screens.narratorSegment: Private data lifecycle management is a key operational concern. blockToLive controls how many blocks private entries remain in the private state DB before peers purge them. Setting blockToLive to zero retains data indefinitely, while a finite value supports temporary secrets like bids. Importantly, purging private data does not remove the public hash from the ledger; the hash remains an immutable proof that the private data once existed. DelPrivateData can be called by chaincode to remove private data from peers' private DBs, but again the public hash will still indicate the historical presence of the data. This distinction matters for compliance and privacy: if your policy requires complete removal of evidence, recognize Fabric's model keeps hashes forever. Another consideration is that purging can lead to authorization confusion: a peer that is later authorized but has purged private data will observe the ledger hash but not hold the content. Fabric includes mechanisms to reconcile this using state replication out-of-band, but plan for retention and recovery in your network governance. In tests, simulate block expiry to observe the purge behavior and confirm your application handles not-found scenarios gracefully.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Retention and deletion
Retention controls
  • blockToLive defines how many blocks private data persists on private DB before automatic purge.
  • Zero means keep the private data forever.
  • DelPrivateData removes private DB entry but does not remove the public hash.
Implications

Even when private data is purged, the public hash remains on the ledger. That hash proves the data existed, which may or may not meet regulatory deletion requirements. Plan retention policies with governance in mind.

Test idea

Set blockToLive to a small value in a testnet and confirm that private entries are purged while the ledger hash remains visible.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes recur when implementing PDCs. First, misconfigured policies—often a mistyped MSP ID—prevent intended peers from receiving private data; always verify policy strings against actual MSP IDs. Second, treating the transient map as optional can leak confidential data: transient must be used for inputs that should never appear on the public ledger. Third, misunderstanding endorsement vs collection policy leads to incorrect assumptions: endorsement governs transaction validity, while collection policies govern distribution of private payloads. Fourth, forgetting to pass the collections file during chaincode commit means peers won't learn collection metadata and private data flows will fail. Finally, assuming DelPrivateData removes the public trace is incorrect—the public hash remains. To avoid these problems, run small tests: deploy with collections, perform PutPrivateData from an authorized client using transient input, read from an authorized peer, and confirm an unauthorized peer cannot retrieve the data. Instrumenting clear, descriptive errors in chaincode will make operational debugging far simpler than sifting through logs alone. Common mistakes and safety notes means check msp ids, use transient for sensitive inputs, include collections at commit, and understand endorsement vs collection policy differences.. In practical terms, misconfigured policies, transient misuse, and endorsement pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In permissioned blockchains, knowing the participants doesn't automatically solve confidentiality. Private Data Collections let a subset of channel members exchange sensitive information peer-to-peer while the channel ledger remains auditable. In this lesson you will learn why PDCs exist, how Fabric keeps private data off the public world state, and how a hash on the public ledger preserves integrity without revealing secrets. We will also walk through how to configure collections, how chaincode stores and retrieves private records, and common operational pitfalls to avoid. Picture a supply chain where price or reserve offers must remain visible only to trading partners: PDCs make that selective sharing practical. By the end you will be able to define a collection in a collections. json file, call PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData from chaincode, and reason about the trade-offs between privacy, auditability and data lifecycle. As you progress, think about which parts of an application truly need persistent privacy and which can remain public. That decision guides your collection design and operational choices.

Over this chapter you will gain four practical competencies that make you confident designing and using Private Data Collections. First, you will explain when PDCs are necessary and list common use cases, including selective sharing in supply chains and financial consortia. Knowing the why helps you avoid overuse. Second, you will define collections in a collection_config. json file: you will identify the name, membership policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, and blockToLive, and understand how these settings affect distribution and retention. Third, you will implement chaincode to interact with private collections using PutPrivateData, GetPrivateData and DelPrivateData, and you will learn to use the transient field to keep inputs out of the public ledger. Fourth, you will analyze how private data affects the ledger: where private state lives, what the public hash guarantees, and how mismatched state or misconfigured policies can invalidate transactions. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can check competency with a concrete task, such as writing a collections. json and demonstrating GetPrivateData from an authorized peer.

These practical checks turn knowledge into demonstrable skills. For configuration, create a collections. json that names a collection, sets an OR-style policy for member MSPs, and chooses required and maximum peer counts; deploy a chaincode commit that uses the file and confirm no errors appear. For code, add functions that marshal a private struct and call PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData; then run a test where an authorized peer reads the private record and an unauthorized peer cannot. For transient usage, send input in a transient map and confirm that the private content never appears in the transaction payload recorded in the public ledger; only a hash is present. For lifecycle, set blockToLive in one collection and observe that peers purge the private entry after the specified number of blocks in a controlled test network. Each check focuses on a single failure mode so you can isolate issues: wrong MSP IDs, incorrect commit flags, or passing confidential data in the public payload. These checks are short, repeatable, and directly validate the learning objectives.

Hyperledger Fabric channels provide a shared ledger where every organization's peers see the world state. That model is simple and powerful, but it isn't sufficient when business rules require selective confidentiality. Private Data Collections exist to fill that gap. A PDC is a logical collection defined on a channel that limits which peers receive and store certain data. The private data itself lives in a private state database on authorized peers, while Fabric stores a hash of that private data on the public ledger. That hash provides immutable evidence that a transaction involving private data occurred, so the network retains verifiability without exposing secrets. Consider a manufacturer and a supplier negotiating raw material costs: price should be private to the negotiating parties while shipment IDs remain public for tracking. PDCs enable exactly that. A common misconception is to treat PDCs as encryption; they are not encryption services. PDC access is governed by membership and endorsement rules. If you need stronger protection in transit or at rest, combine PDCs with TLS and storage encryption, but rely on the PDC model for selective distribution and auditability. When designing a network, decide which attributes must be private and which can be public; that decision drives collection membership and policy design.

Fabric separates the storage of private content from the public world state. Authorized peers keep private entries in a private state database, such as CouchDB or LevelDB. When a transaction includes private data, Fabric writes the private content to those peers' private state DB and computes a hash of that content to be written into the public ledger. That hash acts as an immutable proof linking the public transaction to private content without exposing it. If a peer later tries to commit a transaction whose private data hash does not match the hash on the ledger, the transaction will be marked invalid. This automatic consistency check prevents tampering or mismatched state between peers. Another important architectural point is that the collection's policy controls who receives the private payload during endorsement and commit. Endorsement policies for the chaincode still apply to the transaction; the PDC policy controls distribution of the private data, not endorsement. A misconception is to assume the PDC policy replaces endorsement rules. They operate independently: endorsements decide whether a transaction is valid; collection policies decide which peers store and can query the private data. Think of the public hash as a commitment and the private state DB as the secure vault.

The collection configuration file is the authoritative definition of a Private Data Collection. Each field has operational consequences you must consider. The name is a unique identifier used by chaincode when calling PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData. The policy is an endorsement-style expression that lists member MSP IDs; it determines which organizations are authorized to receive and store private data. requiredPeerCount is the minimum number of peers that must successfully commit private data for the write to be considered validated; set it to a value that reflects your durability needs. maxPeerCount limits how many peers will receive the private payload—useful to reduce exposure. blockToLive sets the lifespan of private entries in the private DB in blocks; zero means retain forever, while a non-zero value will cause automatic purging after the specified number of blocks. Picking blockToLive helps meet privacy or retention requirements but remember that the public hash remains on the ledger even after private data is purged. Common mistakes include incorrect MSP IDs in the policy that prevent rightful members from accessing data and inconsistent counts that cause unexpected commit failures. Always validate your policy strings and test access from each intended member before deploying to production.

Let's look at a concrete collections. json example and interpret it. The file can define multiple collection objects. The first collection, named assetPrivateDetailsCollection, uses a policy allowing Org1 and Org2 members, sets requiredPeerCount to one and maxPeerCount to two, and keeps private data indefinitely with blockToLive set to zero. This setup suits a durable private record shared by two organizations. The second collection, assetBidCollection, allows Org2 and Org3 and sets blockToLive to one hundred blocks, which is useful for temporary bidding information that should expire. When you commit chaincode that uses these collections, include the file via the --collections-config flag. A common error is forgetting to include the file during chaincode commit, which means peers will not have the collection metadata and private data distribution will fail. Also, collection names must match what chaincode uses when calling PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData; otherwise the chaincode will fail to find the collection. Use this example as a template and adjust policies and retention to your business rules. Example collections.json means example shows one persistent collection for private details and one temporary collection for bids with a limited blocktolive.. In practical terms, two collections with different lifetimes and membership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chaincode interacts with Private Data Collections through a small set of specialized APIs provided by the stub. PutPrivateData stores a value under a key in a named collection, GetPrivateData retrieves that private value for authorized peers, and DelPrivateData removes it from the private state database. These calls behave like PutState/GetState/DelState but are scoped to a collection. It is important to pass private inputs via the client transient map for confidentiality; the chaincode should read sensitive fields from the transient map and then call PutPrivateData. If you pass sensitive data directly as transaction arguments, those arguments may be visible in transaction proposals and could be recorded or exposed. Another critical point is error handling: GetPrivateData can return nil when the private value is not found or the peer is not authorized; chaincode should return clear errors in that case. Finally, remember that DelPrivateData only deletes the private entry from private DB—the hash remains on the ledger. Use these APIs consistently and combine them with proper authorization checks, such as verifying the client's MSP ID before writing private details. When you deploy or upgrade chaincode that uses Private Data Collections, the lifecycle commit step must be supplied with the collections configuration file. The peer lifecycle chaincode commit command accepts a --collections-config flag pointing to your collections. json. This ensures that peers in the channel record the collection metadata as part of the chaincode definition and know which peers should receive private payloads. If you omit the collections file at commit time, peers will not have the collection definition and private data operations will fail at runtime. Private data lifecycle management is a key operational concern. blockToLive controls how many blocks private entries remain in the private state DB before peers purge them. Setting blockToLive to zero retains data indefinitely, while a finite value supports temporary secrets like bids. Importantly, purging private data does not remove the public hash from the ledger; the hash remains an immutable proof that the private data once existed. DelPrivateData can be called by chaincode to remove private data from peers' private DBs, but again the public hash will still indicate the historical presence of the data. This distinction matters for compliance and privacy: if your policy requires complete removal of evidence, recognize Fabric's model keeps hashes forever. Another consideration is that purging can lead to authorization confusion: a peer that is later authorized but has purged private data will observe the ledger hash but not hold the content. Fabric includes mechanisms to reconcile this using state replication out-of-band, but plan for retention and recovery in your network governance. In tests, simulate block expiry to observe the purge behavior and confirm your application handles not-found scenarios gracefully.

Several common mistakes recur when implementing PDCs. First, misconfigured policies—often a mistyped MSP ID—prevent intended peers from receiving private data; always verify policy strings against actual MSP IDs. Second, treating the transient map as optional can leak confidential data: transient must be used for inputs that should never appear on the public ledger. Third, misunderstanding endorsement vs collection policy leads to incorrect assumptions: endorsement governs transaction validity, while collection policies govern distribution of private payloads. Fourth, forgetting to pass the collections file during chaincode commit means peers won't learn collection metadata and private data flows will fail. Finally, assuming DelPrivateData removes the public trace is incorrect—the public hash remains. To avoid these problems, run small tests: deploy with collections, perform PutPrivateData from an authorized client using transient input, read from an authorized peer, and confirm an unauthorized peer cannot retrieve the data. Instrumenting clear, descriptive errors in chaincode will make operational debugging far simpler than sifting through logs alone. Let's consolidate the most important points. A Private Data Collection is a Fabric feature that lets a subset of organizations store and share confidential data peer-to-peer while committing a hash to the public ledger for verification. The collection_config. json file is the configuration artifact where you name collections, set membership policies, define required and maximum peer counts, and set blockToLive for retention.
